title: The Four Noble Truths, Part 3
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the Noble Eightfold Path in part three of a series on the Four Noble Truths, drawing on Thanissaro Bhikkhu's booklet The Noble Eightfold Path. Kanho describes the path as a wheel with eight spokes around a common center, where working through them one at a time risks getting stuck at right view. Kanho then covers the wisdom category of right view and right intention, asking when life is on the freeway, on the frontage road, or in the blackberry brambles. Right speech gets the longest treatment, including the five conditions from the Patimokkha for admonishing another: right time, facts, gentleness, profitable words, and a kindly heart. The evening ends with a paired listening exercise on discernment.

sentences.text: Good evening.
Welcome to part three of our investigation of the Four Noble Truths.
Tonight we will begin to look at the actual mechanics of liberation, the Noble Eightfold Path.
For this talk I have leaned on the booklet *The Noble Eightfold Path* by Thanissaro Bhikkhu.
If you have not seen that booklet yet, please check the library.
There may be a few copies left.
The Noble Eightfold Path is part of the Four Noble Truths.
So what are the Four Noble Truths?
They are the first teaching that the Buddha gave, also known as the First Turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
He said that this teaching was for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world.
In this spirit, let us see what the Buddha told his disciples.
*Now this bhikkhus is the Noble Truth of suffering.

Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, union with what is displeasing is suffering, separation from what is pleasing is suffering, not to get what one wants is suffering.
In brief, the five aggregates, subject to clinging, are suffering.*
*Now this bhikkhus is the Noble Truth of the origin of suffering.

It is this craving which leads to re-becoming, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there, that is craving for sensual pleasures, craving for becoming, craving for this becoming.*
*Now this bhikkhus is the Noble Truth of the cessation of suffering.
It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, non-reliance on it.*
*Now this bhikkhus is the Noble Truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
It is this Noble Eightfold Path that is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.*
I should mention that the "right" in the Eightfold Path is sometimes translated as "perfect."
As we know, there are issues with the word "right" and with the word "perfect."
But we do need a way of talking about all this.
So let's just take this "right" as the placeholder for a non-dualistic right, not right and wrong, but just the right feeling about it.
That's the hazard when we use words, right?
The path is often depicted as a wheel with eight spokes coming from a common center.
This means we don't have to perfect one spoke or one branch and then step on to the next, working our way through all eight in a serial fashion.
There's actually even a danger in that.
The danger is we might get stuck with right view, never have the perfect right view, and never move away from it, and so never leave the starting block.

The other danger may lie in thinking, "I have perfected the right view and now I'm working on the right intention," and never looking back to see if our perception of the right view has shifted or whether we need to look at it again.
Other teachers say that the elements of the right path are building blocks.
How can one practice morality when our view and our aspiration are not developed?
In short, I think the answer to that is that while we may emphasize a certain practice at any given time, the goal is to embody the totality of the path.
The truth of the end of suffering, the path, is personal.
It's not magic, and it's not only available to some special people, something mystic.
No, it is actually the promise of our practice.
Looking at my life, I need to ask this question: how much of it is on the path?
When am I on the frontage road?
When am I bushwhacking?
When am I just plain lost?
When I check in with myself about these things, there is usually a part of me that knows exactly what it means to be on the path.
And there is also a part of me that prefers short-time soothing of anxiety and not dealing with the actual malady.
So let me repeat the different spokes or branches of the path.
*Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
It is the noble eightfold path that is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.*
Often the Eightfold Path is split into three categories.
Wisdom or discernment includes right view and right intention.
Some people also call it right resolve.
Moral virtue includes right speech, right action and right livelihood.
The third category is meditation and includes right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration.
Hearing this, we might think about getting the good stuff, the right stuff.
And yet, when we hang out with it a bit longer and think about it more, we might see that often it is not about getting, but getting rid of: abandoning unskillful habits and mind states.
Sometimes the Four Noble Truths are translated as the truths for the noble ones.
And the Buddha asks of us, as noble ones, to learn how to delight in abandoning whatever we need to abandon and to delight in developing whatever needs to be developed.
Therefore, noble ones, let us look at the first category, which is wisdom or discernment.
Wisdom can sound intimidating, and I have a preference for discernment because that is something we do all the time, and why not do it in relationship to the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path?
The first spoke of the wheel is right view, and it is part of the discernment category.
We practice right view to clear confusion, misunderstanding and deluded thinking.
It is a means to gain right understanding of reality.
We understand and observe that our actions have consequences.
Traditional Buddhist teaching includes that our actions and beliefs also have consequences after death by determining the shape of our rebirth.
Mundane right view is a knowledge of the fruits of good behavior.
Having this type of view will bring merit and will support the favorable rebirth of the sentient being in the realm of samsara.
Right view is important because it underlies all of our efforts to stay on the path.
It colors the way we look at everything.
The second spoke of the wheel is right intention.
It also belongs in the wisdom category.
Right understanding is the understanding of things as they are, and in this context the Four Noble Truths are the explanation of how things are.
It is not a scientific explanation of the universe or anything modern.
It is not psychology.
It loops back to the Buddha's first talk.
From my life I know that the power of choice is not enough.
Sometimes I get tired and grouchy, fed up with what I see and hear, with politics, with news, with physical pain, with mental pain.
Three or four days of insomnia and the world does not look so good to me.
Actions based on that momentary state of mind do not have good outcomes.
Remember what I said about the path?
Acting with that frame of mind has me leave the freeway and launch myself into the blackberry brambles and then complain about the thorns.
So I must be prepared for that with a bigger plan.
I must practice the skills that go along with it.
My unskillful actions cause trouble for myself and for those around me.
If I practice and if I remember it, I have room to make decisions.
I have room every time I encounter a person, a thing, an action.
I have the room to make decisions beyond or outside of my current emotional and mental state.
The key is to have enough distance from the current upheaval so I can remember.
Am I causing harm?
This is very important.
Am I willing to admit to myself that I am causing harm?
Or do I tell myself that they had it coming anyways?
This honesty is demanding and not to be taken lightly.
It requires that we have a good understanding of dukkha in our life.
The shape suffering takes in our life is personal, and as long as we are blind to its shape we continue to mislead ourselves and to misbehave.
Right intention includes my intention to meditate.
From the place I hold during meditation I also hold the ability and skill to see myself and my actions in a different fashion.

I gain greater distance from the continuous battering from my ego, the non-stop "I want this, I don't want that," and what is going on, and maybe I get a different grasp on how my actions impact the world around me.
The third spoke of the wheel is right speech.
Right speech is the first of the morality teachings.
It includes external speech, but it also includes internal speech.
Here the practice of abandonment should be a strong one.
Most often I cause trouble not by leaving things unsaid but by saying that which is basically unskillful and ego-driven.
Gaining skill with right speech, with what we say and how we say it, helps with the internal chatter too.
I don't remember where I found the following quote.
I wrote it in my notebook without listing the source.

*Right speech means abstention, one, from telling lies; two, from backbiting and slander and talk that may bring about hatred, enmity, disunity and disharmony among individuals or groups of people; three, from harsh, rude, impolite, malicious and abusive language; and four, from idle, useless and foolish babble and gossip.
When one abstains from these forms of wrong and harmful speech, one naturally has to speak the truth, has to use words that are friendly and benevolent.*
The Buddha was not quite using that modern language, but he placed five conditions on right speech, especially when we are about to admonish another.
*The Buddha said, "And what other five conditions must be established in himself?"
Do I speak at the right time or not?
Do I speak of the facts or not?
Do I speak gently or harshly?
Do I speak profitable words or not?
Do I speak with a kindly heart or inwardly malicious?*
Sorry for the gender-oriented language here.
That's from the Patimokka translated by Nanamoli Thera.
So I have spent a lot of time on right speech because this is where being unskillful really hurts other people, and it also hurts us.
I would like to stop here because I would like to keep enough time for a little bit of small group discussion.
Is there anybody here who hasn't done that yet in the past?
Show of hands?
Great.
So small group discussion works like this.
Two people, maybe people who don't hang out with each other all the time, get together, and one person speaks at a time.
I will start signaling with this in four minutes, and during those four minutes the other person is silent and just really listens.
One key is not to formulate our responses or replies or comments while the other person is speaking.
We really try to listen with all we got.
When I ring the bell, please finish your sentence and then it's the other person's turn.
When I ring the third time, please come back to your old spot and we'll chat together a little bit.
One last thing: please treat what you hear with respect and confidentiality.
So the question is this: what has come up for you around the practice or the investigation, or during the talk, about discernment?
So right view and right understanding.
If you want to spread out, find a partner so we can start our conversation.
Anybody without a partner?
The practice or investigation of discernment.
